title: A Report Is Not an Overlay
description: A 23 December 2025 test vault can cite and extract. It cannot yet keep agreements, events, and evidence alive as the work changes.
body:
A knowledge system that produces a one-time report about a vault has not yet learned to live beside the vault. The report is useful once. The work continues. Amendments arrive. Submissions miss their window. If the memory cannot move when the files move, you are back to searching folders.

On 23 December 2025 I test VALESKA against a realistic petroleum-governance case: a deliberately fragmented set of agreements, amendments, submissions, approvals, and audit records. It is an emulation, not a deployment for a government. The question is whether a working proof of concept is the same thing as a living overlay. The files already say it is not.

What the vault actually is

The test collection is synthetic markdown, not a live ECM. Five instruments. Scripts that stamp a SHA-256 and a git SHA so a citation stays put. Regex harvest of obligations. A compliance report that can match some evidence to those obligations. On that day the count is 44 obligations, five evidence records, three matches, forty still waiting. Citation stability works. A small collection can yield obligations. That is Gate 2 and Gate 3 as a proof of concept. It is not a government system of record.

The emulation is still the right patient. Research into how petroleum files actually sit in a ministry — departmental shares, mailboxes, scanned PDFs, final_FINAL.docx versioning — is why the overlay idea exists. Most people browse the share they already have. They do not have a node identifier. VALESKA has to make identity with hashes and history when the source environment has none to give.

The gap is the finding

The same day’s gap analysis is more useful than a success narrative. There is no persistent agreement state. There is no event history. There is no living obligation register. Static JSON and one-time scripts do not update when a later amendment arrives. A file share, a mailbox, or a content platform has no contract for telling VALESKA that something changed. A list of obligations is not a system that can calculate a deadline, mark missing evidence, and explain a risk signal in conservative language.

I am not going to reshape the general VALESKA database in place to fake that overlay. Discovery and semantic retrieval remain the general system’s job. A governance overlay needs its own model: agreements, evidence, citations, events, obligations, risk signals, documented exceptions. That is still an overlay. It should reference source material through stable identifiers. It should not copy a customer’s records into a new cabinet and call the copy the truth.

Where an enterprise content system exists, that identifier may already be a node id. Where the source environment is shares, mailboxes, and informal version names, VALESKA has to mint identity with hashes and history. The demo used local markdown because that is how the emulation is built. The gap analysis is explicit: without a database of agreements and events, there is no overlay, only a parser with a report.

The next test

The work is no longer only how to extract from documents. It is how decisions, obligations, evidence, and events stay connected as the underlying work changes. Until there is a durable model, an event path, and an integration contract, this remains a report about a vault. The architecture still has to live beside the work.

Historical basis: VALESKA commit 85c9366, December 23, 2025; contemporaneous gap analysis, emulation rationale, connection log, and synthetic test-vault scripts. Counts (5 documents, 44 obligations, 3 matched) are from the 23 December demo report.

data.author: David Gargan
data.coverAlt: A night vault with a steel door, sealed documents, a wall map, and a chain of glowing records across a marble table: an overlay that has to live beside the source, not a one-time report.
